items.stem: What does O(n log n) describe for a comparison sort?

options.text: A lower bound no comparison sort can beat in the worst case
options.rationale: Correct: comparison sorts cannot do better than n log n in the worst case.

options.text: The exact number of comparisons for every input
options.rationale: Big-O is an asymptotic bound, not an exact count.
It describes time growth, not space.

options.text: That the sort is always faster than O(n^2) for all inputs
options.rationale: For small or special inputs an O(n^2) sort can be faster.

items.explanation: Correct: comparison sorts cannot do better than n log n in the worst case.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about hash tables are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Average lookup is O(1) with a good hash and load factor
options.rationale: Correct: amortised O(1) under good conditions.

options.text: Worst-case lookup can degrade to O(n) with many collisions
options.rationale: Correct: pathological collisions linearise the bucket.

options.text: They keep keys in sorted order
options.rationale: Hash tables do not maintain sorted order.

options.text: They guarantee O(1) in every case
options.rationale: No such guarantee; collisions break it.

items.explanation: Correct: amortised O(1) under good conditions.

items.stem: Why memoise in a dynamic-programming solution?

options.text: To change the problem's optimal answer
options.rationale: It does not change the answer, only the work done.

options.text: To reduce the number of distinct subproblems
options.rationale: The set of subproblems is unchanged.
